structure.title: Refusal and arrest
structure.text: Pentheus confronts the new worship spreading through Thebes and attempts to bring its stranger under control.

structure.title: Curiosity and exposure
structure.text: The encounters draw hidden desires into public consequences, while reports from the mountain change the scale of the conflict.

people.name: Dionysus
people.text: The god of wine and ecstasy, returning disguised as a mortal to his mother's city of Thebes, which has refused to honour him.

people.name: Pentheus
people.text: Thebes' young king, Dionysus' cousin, who is determined to stamp out the new worship and sees only disorder in it.

people.name: The Bacchae
people.text: The women who have left their homes for the mountains to worship Dionysus, and whose rites the city's men do not understand.

context.title: Divine recognition
context.text: Dionysus demands acknowledgment of his divinity. His power and his treatment of people raise different questions; power alone does not settle moral judgment.

context.title: Outside the city
context.text: The mountain offers an alternative to the ruler's ordered spaces. Reports of it mix attraction, fear, and claims about what has been seen.
context.takeaway: Ask how distance shapes each account.

notice.why: Pentheus may be attracted to what he claims only to police.
Identity becomes vulnerable when someone else arranges the scene.

opening: A new religious frenzy has drawn the women of Thebes out into the mountains, and King Pentheus intends to restore order. The stranger encouraging it seems an easy person to arrest. What Pentheus does not understand is that the god he refuses to acknowledge is present, enjoying the encounter, and attentive to the curiosity beneath his outrage. Euripides brings desire, humiliation, and divine power into a confrontation where the ruler's determination to expose other people's madness makes him increasingly available for manipulation.
